newsitem.title: UK: Russia bond oversubscribed, spread could tighten.
newsitem.headline: Russia bond oversubscribed, spread could tighten.

text.p: Russia's $1.0 billion five-year Eurobond launched on Thursday was heavily oversubscribed and the spread should tighten after pricing, syndicate officials said.
"The bond was oversubscribed and we saw good investor demand across-the-board," a syndicate source close to the deal said.
He expected the Eurobond spread would tighten by up to 15 basis points once it was freed to trade. "It could go to 330 b.p. What we don't want is the spread to tighten to 300 b.p."
The Eurobond will be priced to yield 345 b.p. over the new five-year U.S. Treasury note later today via joint lead managers J.P. Morgan and SBC Warburg.
The T-note was trading at a 5.93 percent yield in London.
That yield meant the Russian Eurobond would likely pay a semi-annual coupon of 9.25 percent, dealers said.
"Roughly we sold about 45 percent into the U.S., 30 percent into Asia and 25 percent into Europe," the syndicate source said, adding there was good demand in Korea and Hong Kong.
"There was institutional fund interest, demand from banks, significant retail interest, insurance companies and mutual funds," he said.
The deal was unlikely to be increased despite overwhelming investor demand, dealers said.
"Yes, the spread will most probably tighten. On a deal that is so oversubscribed you generally see the spread tightening when it first comes out," a new issues trader said.
"Everyone involved should see this as a resounding success for the Russians, for investors across-the-board," he added.
Originally, the market expected up to $500 million. As recently as Wednesday, bankers were talking about $750 million.
The increases followed a promotional extravaganza in which three teams of Russian officials and bankers spanned 14 cities in less than two weeks.
Investors and bankers flocked to a presentation in London last Friday where Russia's finance minister Alexander Livshits said he wanted the Eurobond to show the country was a respectable borrower.
The marketing campaign started in Tokyo and culminated in New York on Wednesday.
The Eurobond was the country's first international bond offering since the 1917 revolution and has been discussed for some two years.
Russia is rated Ba2 by Moody's Investors Service and BB minus by Standard & Poor's, which are below investment grade but were at the top end of market expectations when assigned in October.
